title: Enhanced Superconductivity in Multilayer FeSe Films by Simplified Molecular Beam Epitaxy
authors: Maria Hilse, Hemian Yi, Zhe Chen, Jessica L. Thompson, Kalana D. Halanayake, Danielle Reifsnyder Hickey, Seong H. Kim, Cui-Zu Chang, Nitin Samarth, Roman Engel-Herbert
abstract: Multi-unit-cell (UC) \b{eta}-FeSe films grown on SrTiO3(100) continue to attract attention because of the significant enhancement in the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) compared to that in bulk FeSe. In prior reports of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)-grown \b{eta}-FeSe/SrTiO3(100), elaborate growth protocols have been used to achieve enhanced Tc, leading to a general belief that careful pre-treatment of the SrTiO3 substrate and post-growth annealing in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) are essential. Here, we report a greatly simplified protocol for the MBE growth of superconducting multi-UC \b{eta}-FeSe films on SrTiO3(100), eliminating the need for careful substrate pre-treatment and post-growth UHV annealing while still achieving an enhanced Tc. With appropriate capping, epitaxial films with 14 UC thickness exhibit a zero-resistance transition temperature Tc ~ 20 K in ex situ electrical transport measurements. The MBE optimization process is guided by the growth-parameter dependencies of film morphology and structural properties, as characterized by reflection high-energy electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and scanning transmission electron microscopy.
summary: This work reports a breakthrough in synthesizing superconducting FeSe films by developing a greatly simplified MBE growth protocol. By eliminating complex substrate pre-treatments and post-growth annealing, the authors achieved high-quality, multi-unit-cell films exhibiting a high superconducting transition temperature of $\sim 20 	ext{ K}$. This significantly advances the practical synthesis of high-temperature superconducting materials.
main_problem: The primary goal is to achieve enhanced superconductivity in multilayer beta-FeSe films while significantly simplifying the complex molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth protocols previously required.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an enhanced superconducting transition temperature ($T_c \sim 20 	ext{ K}$) in 14-unit-cell films using a greatly simplified MBE protocol that eliminates the need for substrate pre-treatment or post-growth UHV annealing.
method: The study employs MBE growth techniques coupled with extensive characterization, including AFM, RHEED, XRD, and ex situ electrical transport measurements, to correlate growth parameters with film quality and superconducting properties.
model_or_system: The physical system is multi-unit-cell (UC) beta-FeSe films epitaxially grown on SrTiO3(100) substrates. The research focuses on controlling the film's stoichiometry and crystalline quality to maximize the superconducting transition temperature.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), root mean square (rms) roughness (AFM), XRD peak width (FWHM), and sheet resistance.
important_parameters: Growth Temperature ($T_{	ext{GG}}$), Se/Fe flux ratio (FR), and film thickness (up to 14 UC).
main_assumptions: The authors challenge the prior understanding that elaborate protocols (pre-treatment, annealing) are strictly necessary for high-$T_c$ FeSe films.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of AFM surface morphology on growth temperature and Se/Fe FR, while XRD scans track changes in crystallinity (peak width) across different growth conditions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the background on enhanced $T_c$ in FeSe, presents the novel simplified growth protocol, details the characterization of morphology and structure using multiple techniques, and concludes with the measurement of high $T_c$ values.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state superconductivity, the detailed control over epitaxial growth, stoichiometry, and structural transitions (e.g., island vs. layer-by-layer growth) provides valuable experimental insights into achieving highly ordered quantum materials, which is relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in artificial quantum systems.
